items.title: On adjoint orbits in nilpotent ideals of a Borel subalgebra: the intersection theorem (Theorem 3.2)
items.published_title: On adjoint orbits in nilpotent ideals of a Borel subalgebra: the intersection theorem (Theorem 3.2)
items.author: Rupert W. T. Yu
items.difficulty_reason:
Counted unit: the paper's intersection theorem for closed Borel-stable subsets, printed as Theorem 3.2 of the paper (source0.tex lines 330--333), delivered together with the paper's own complete proof of it at source0.tex lines 334--404. The statement is that the intersection of two non empty closed B-stable subsets of m^bullet is non empty, for an arbitrary nilpotent ideal m of the Borel subalgebra b of a complex finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra; it is the theorem that supplies the uniqueness half of the paper's main result (the abstract's unique closed B-orbit in m^bullet), and the paper's own stated main result (printed as Theorem 1.1, source0.tex lines 106--111) carries no proof anywhere in the paper, so the counted unit is the paper's main proved theorem rather than a formal restatement of an unproved one.

The author's proof is complete and is carried out at the level of coordinate rings. After localising the coordinate ring of m at the product phi of the coordinate functions attached to the minimal roots of m, and identifying m^bullet with the non-vanishing locus of phi, the author splits the coordinate ring of m^bullet as the coordinate ring of m_0^bullet plus the kernel of the comorphism of the projection, using the B_0-equivariant projection of m^bullet onto m_0^bullet. Taking a proper B-stable ideal J, the author observes that its image is a B_0-stable ideal in the coordinate ring of m_0^bullet, where the open B_0-orbit of m_0 (Richardson) forces that image to be either zero or the whole ring. In the second case the author uses that the group M_0 with Lie algebra m_0 is unipotent to average an element f of J with f + g equal to the constant 1 along M_0, obtaining non constant elements f-tilde in the m_0-invariants of J and g-tilde in the m_0-invariants of the kernel whose sum is a constant; the weight decomposition in the negative semi-group generated by the minimal roots, together with the proposition proved immediately before the counted theorem (that those invariants reduce to the polynomial ring on the minimal-root coordinates), lets the author multiply g-tilde by a power of phi and land inside that polynomial ring, which is impossible for a non zero element of the kernel. Hence the image of every proper B-stable ideal is zero. The conclusion is the ideal-theoretic form of the statement: two proper B-stable ideals can never sum to the unit ideal, so two non empty closed B-stable subsets of m^bullet must meet.

Carrying this out requires the invariant theory of unipotent group actions, the dense-orbit theorem of Richardson and the theorem of Rosenlicht that the B-invariant rational functions on m_0 are constant, the weight bookkeeping for semi-invariant regular functions with weights in the negative semi-group generated by the minimal roots, the localisation dictionary between the open subset m^bullet and its coordinate ring, and the translation between closed B-stable subsets and B-stable ideals. No qualifying examination poses this: the argument is the technical heart of a research paper on B-orbits in nilpotent ideals, it is stated for an arbitrary nilpotent ideal in an arbitrary type, and the paper's introduction says that no such general statement was available in the literature. That places the unit in the upper qualifying-to-research range: H2.

items.difficulty_reason:
Counted unit: the paper's robust-control proposition for the nonlinear affine-in-control system, printed as the second of the paper's two Propositions (source0.tex lines 440--443), delivered together with the paper's own complete proof of it at source0.tex lines 444--457. The statement is that using the control u = u-bar + u_d renders the system x-dot = a(x) + b(x)u + d(t,x) asymptotically stable, where u-bar is a control law assumed to stabilize the undisturbed system with a strictly positive definite Lyapunov function V whose derivative is negative along the undisturbed controlled trajectories, where b(x) has rank n for all x, and where the disturbance is bounded in norm by a known function lambda with |d| strictly below lambda; the robustifying term is u_d = -(lambda/|grad V|) b-dagger grad V with b-dagger the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse.

items.difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the decomposition formula for the discriminant of a homogeneous polynomial invariant under the direct product of two symmetric groups, printed as Theorem 3.2 of the paper (native source0.tex lines 743--788), delivered together with the author's own complete proof of it (source0.tex lines 790--792, a proof environment closed by the author). The statement is one of the two main theorems of the paper: it is the theorem the paper's Example 3.3 immediately specialises to a degree-4 invariant polynomial to produce a factorised discriminant, and it is the four-regime refinement (p<d or p>=d, q<d or q>=d) of the paper's general decomposition formula for resultants, Theorem 2.1. Theorem A is the technical heart of the paper: with the monotonicity Theorem B it yields the three-dimensional Briancon-Iarrobino conjecture (the paper's Corollary 1), and the authors describe it as strengthening the previously known bound up to a factor 4/3 by Ramkumar-Sammartano through a new error term. Why the unit is research-level rather than an ordinary qualifying problem: the proof has to compare hom(I,R/I) with the sum of the graded pieces hom(I_i,S/I_j) and then subtract, for every pair i>j, the number binom(i-j,2) of maps that occur in a bounded connected component but cannot extend to the tangent space; establishing that those maps are exactly the zero vectors requires the paper's Lemma 2.1 (retained with its proof), which uses Borel-fixedness and a strictly negative x-exponent to force gamma + alpha + e_y and gamma + alpha + e_x out of the monomial ideal; the counting is then assembled with the two inequalities hom(J,S/J') <= l + l' - t(J,J') (the paper's Corollary 1.15, retained with the Section 1.6 machinery that defines the spaces A, B and the function t(J,J'), and the paper's Corollary 2.2, retained) and with the double-binomial identity sum_{j} sum_{i>j} binom(i-j,2) = binom(m_1+2,4) applied twice, producing T(I) <= (2m_1+1)l - 2 binom(m_1+2,4). The lemma is the paper's hypothesis-checking result: it gives sufficient conditions on the supply and demand distributions under which the expected hitting times E(M), E(0), the boundary hit probabilities p_M, p_0 and the expected positive and negative parts of the drift are all finite and non-degenerate, and the paper invokes it in exactly that role ("the conditions of Lemma 3 (see Appendix B.1) hold, and H_M and H_0 exist") before every one of its achievability theorems. Part (iii): a one-step return to M happens whenever Z_1 >= epsilon, so p_M >= Pr(Z_1 >= epsilon | S_0 = M) >= delta > 0, while on E^-_L the process hits 0 within the first L rounds before it can return to M, so Pr(S_{tau(M)} = 0 | S_0 = M) >= delta^L and p_M <= 1 - delta^L < 1; the case of p_0 is the symmetric one, and the proof says so. items.difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the growth-rate theorem for the expected number of identifiable admixture components, printed as Theorem 3 of "Finite Admixture Models: a Bridge with Stochastic Geometry and Choquet Theory" (source0.tex lines 421--433, source label growth), delivered together with the article's own complete proof at source0.tex lines 1909--1913, which sits detached in the article's appendix under the heading Proof of Theorem 3 and is bound to the statement here. The theorem is the article's first main result, announced in its abstract (the growth rate of the expected number of identifiable components is found by stochastic convex geometry) and listed in its section on main results as the first of three. It states that for points sampled iid uniformly on the unit simplex the expected number of extremal points of their convex hull, which the article identifies with the number of identifiable admixture components, equals J/(J+1)^{J-1} (log n)^{J-1} plus an error of order (log n)^{J-2} log log n, and consequently that the normalised expectation converges to the constant c(J) = J/(J+1)^{J-1}. The proof is complete and closed inside the retained span and consists of the two steps the theorem needs: it quotes the sharp asymptotic expansion of the expected number of vertices of the convex hull of n points sampled uniformly in a convex polytope P of R^d, namely tau(P)/((d+1)^{d-1}(d-1)!) (log n)^{d-1} + O((log n)^{d-2} log log n), from the two cited results (Reitzner's Theorem 6 and Barany-Buchta's Theorem 5, which the article cites at the point of use and which the retained context also flags), and then verifies that the hypotheses hold for the article's own model, since the unit simplex is a convex polytope in R^J, and computes the only quantity the constant depends on, the number of towers of the simplex, tau(Delta^{J-1}) = (J-1)! J. Substituting gives (J-1)! J / ((J+1)^{J-1} (J-1)!) = J/(J+1)^{J-1}, which is exactly the displayed constant of the theorem, and the second display follows by dividing by (log n)^{J-1}. Every step of the reduction and every hypothesis check is in the retained span, the constant is computed rather than asserted, and the only external inputs are the two named published theorems. The argument is rated H2: the statement is a research result that required recognising that a finite admixture model's identifiable components are the extremal points of a random polytope in the simplex, and the count tau(Delta^{J-1}) = (J-1)! J is a genuine verification, but the proof itself is a short and complete reduction to two deep published theorems rather than an independent technical development, so it is not rated H3. It is nevertheless the strongest claim in the article whose proof the article itself writes out in full and whose dependencies are all retained here: the article's other main results either repeat the same reduction pattern (its Theorems 4, 5 and 8), or are propositions whose proofs the article disables inside conditional-false blocks (its proofs of the apeirogon theorem and of the extremal-posterior theorem), or are stated without proof.

items.author: Daqing Wan and Dingxin Zhang
items.difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the exactness of the rows of the article's Dwork double complex, printed as Lemma 6.7 (source0.tex lines 2570--2574, source label lemma:c-exactness-of-rows), delivered with the article's own complete proof at source0.tex lines 2576--2710 (135 lines). The statement is a chain-level assertion about the double complex (6.5) built from the overconvergent Dwork complex: each of its rows is exact in cohomology degrees 0,1,...,c-1, which is what makes the 0th to (c-1)st columns of the E_1-page of the associated spectral sequence vanish. The proof is a genuine source-local argument rather than a citation: it first replaces the toric double complex by an equivalent affine complex with differentials D_j, reduces exactness of every row to acyclicity of the zeroth row of a smaller double complex, then builds an auxiliary Dwork crystal on a product of formal projective spaces, applies the Baldassarri--Berthelot local comparison theorem, uses the retained Lemma 5.6 to concentrate the local cohomology complex in degree 0, and finally identifies the shifted zeroth row with a relative de Rham complex, which is the claimed acyclicity. The two quoted inputs (the comparison theorem, and the equivalence between overconvergent D-modules and modules over the overconvergent Weyl algebra) are named and retained in the item as statements, and the proof, not the quotation, is the work: this lemma is the technical heart of the paper's Dwork-cohomology method, on which the paper's divisibility theorems rest. H2: an original research lemma with a complete author proof, depending on two quoted external theorems.

items.title: Convergence rate of the (1+1)-evolution strategy on locally strongly convex functions with Lipschitz continuous gradient: the martingale strong-law convergence rate proposition (Proposition 2)
items.published_title: Convergence rate of the (1+1)-evolution strategy on locally strongly convex functions with Lipschitz continuous gradient: the martingale strong-law convergence rate proposition (Proposition 2)
items.author: Daiki Morinaga, Kazuto Fukuchi, Jun Sakuma, Youhei Akimoto
items.difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the article's Proposition 2 (source0.tex lines 455--475, source label prop:convergence_rate), which packages the convergence-rate analysis of the (1+1)-evolution strategy into three checkable conditions on a Markov chain: given a filtration and a Markov chain adapted to it, if C1 (a uniform upper bound on the expected one-step decrement) and C3 (square-summability of the variances divided by t^2) hold, then the almost-sure limsup of (X_t - X_0)/t is at most -B^upper, and if C2 and C3 hold then the almost-sure liminf is at least -B^lower; it is delivered with the article's complete original proof at source0.tex lines 2410--2425 (the appendix subsection "Proof of Proposition 2", 16 lines). The proposition is the article's declared central tool: the article introduces it with the sentence "Our main mathematical tool to derive bounds for the upper and lower convergence rate of the (1+1)-ES is the strong law of large numbers on martingales [7]. It reduces the analysis of the limit behavior to the analysis of the expected sequence change in one step. The following proposition is the central tool for our analysis", and both of the article's main theorems (its upper convergence rate bound and its lower convergence rate bound) are proved by verifying C1--C3 and applying it. The author proof is complete and closed inside the retained span: it forms the martingale difference sequence Z_{t+1} = X_{t+1} - E[X_{t+1} | F_t], decomposes (X_t - X_0)/t into the martingale average plus the average of the conditional expectations, uses the variance decomposition Var[X_t] = Var[Z_t] + Var[E[X_t | F_{t-1}]] >= Var[Z_t] to see that C3 implies the square-summability of E[Z_t^2]/t^2, applies Chow's strong law of large numbers for martingales to get the almost-sure vanishing of the martingale average, and then takes limsup with C1 and liminf with C2 to obtain statements (I) and (II). The argument is short but it is a genuine research-paper step: the choice of the variance condition C3 exactly so that Chow's theorem applies, and the passage from the one-step expected change to the almost-sure asymptotic rate, are the content of the paper's method rather than a routine verification. H2: an original research proposition with a complete author proof, depending on one quoted external theorem (the cited martingale strong law).

items.published_title: Monitoring edge-geodetic sets in graphs: the upper bound in terms of the feedback edge set number (Theorem 4.3)

items.difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the article's Theorem 4.3 (source0.tex lines 384--386, source label thm:fes), "If $\fes(G) \geq 2$, then $\MEG(G) \leq 9\fes(G) + |L(G)| - 8$ where $|L(G)|$ is the number of leaves of $G$", delivered together with the article's complete original proof at source0.tex lines 387--420 (34 lines, a single adjacent proof environment that opens and closes inside the retained span). It is one of the article's two main structural results: the abstract announces that the paper "prove[s] an upper bound using the feedback edge set of the graph", the bound is the source of the article's Corollary 4.4 that $\MEG(G)=O(\MLN(G)^2)$ for every graph, and the article immediately notes after the proof that the bound is best possible up to constant factors, with a matching construction in its Proposition 4.5. The author proof is complete and self-contained apart from the two quoted lemmas it names. It fixes $k=\fes(G)$, describes a set $M$ of vertices of the base graph $G_b$ (all core vertices; one or two median vertices from every proper core path of length at least two; two or three non-core vertices from every core cycle chosen as equidistantly as possible), argues that every edge of a maximal hanging tree is monitored by leaves through the simplicial-vertex and cut-vertex lemmas, then verifies edge by edge that $M$ monitors the edges on core cycles (via the cut-vertex lemma and the cycle theorem) and on proper core paths (through the medians $x_1,x_2$ and the distance computation $d$ versus at least $d+1$ for any alternative path), and finally counts $|M| \leq 3n_c+2n_p+2k-2 \leq 3k+2(2k-3)+2k-2 = 9k-8$ using the quoted bound of at most $2k-2$ core vertices and at most $3k-3$ core paths, adding the $|L(G)|$ leaves by the retained Lemma 4.2. The construction and its verification, in particular the equidistant placement of two or three vertices on each core cycle and the worst-case counting over core cycles and core paths, are research-level graph-structural arguments rather than routine exercises, and the two quoted lemmas are named published results. items.title: The collection of weights of generalized metric tree arrangements is the Dressian Dr(k,n)
items.published_title: The collection of weights of generalized metric tree arrangements is the Dressian Dr(k,n)
items.author: Ayush Kumar Tewari
items.difficulty_reason: The counted theorem is the headline result of the article's fourth section and of its abstract, and its twelve-line author proof is a genuine research-level set equality rather than a qualification exercise. Even with the whole apparatus of the delivered context supplied - the Dressian Dr(k,n) as the tropical prevariety of the three-term Plucker relations, the phylogenetic and tree-distance definitions, the definition of a metric tree arrangement and of an abstract tree arrangement, Lemma lem:mat_sub_k,n with its complete proof, and above all the author's own definition of a generalized metric tree arrangement with its compatibility equation and the induced weight vector w_T - the solver must still do the following. For the forward inclusion it must recognise that a fixed three-term tropical Plucker relation for Dr(k,n) is indexed by a (k-2)-subset J together with four distinct indices outside J, identify the family S of k-subsets containing J, observe that S is in bijection with the two-subsets of the complement of J so that the restriction of w_T to those Plucker variables is exactly the weight induced by the single metric tree T_J, and then import Speyer-Sturmfels' identification of the weights induced by metric trees on n-k+2 leaves with Dr(2,n-k+2) in order to conclude that the maximum of the relation is attained by at least two of its three terms. For the reverse inclusion it must run the construction the other way: from an arbitrary w in Dr(k,n), restrict w along each (k-2)-subset J, read the restricted Plucker variables as a weight on the two-subsets of the complement of J, obtain a point of Dr(2,n-k+2), invoke the same metric-tree representation to produce a tree T_J on those leaves, and then verify that the resulting family of trees satisfies the compatibility condition - which is the point where the author's definition has to be recognised as having been designed to make w_T well defined, since all the trees are cut out of one and the same point w. This mutual reduction between a single generalized object and a whole family of rank-two Dressians, plus the well-definedness argument that carries the definition, is well beyond ordinary PhD qualifying examinations in tropical geometry.

items.difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the article's Proposition 4.5.1 (source0.tex lines 1687--1691, source label prop:PrimeField), "Suppose that Theorem Noetherianity holds when $K$ is a prime field. Then it also holds when $K$ is an arbitrary finite field", delivered with the article's complete original proof at source0.tex lines 1693--1715 (23 lines, one adjacent proof environment that opens and closes inside the retained span). The proposition is the pivot of the article's proof of its main Noetherianity theorem: the paper immediately records in a boxed remark (retained, lines 1717--1723) that "In view of Proposition~\ref{prop:PrimeField}, from now on we assume that $K$ is a prime field", and the rest of the proof of Noetherianity (the embedding theorem and the shift theorem, sections 4.6--4.8) is carried out only under that assumption. The author proof is complete and self-contained: it passes from the finite field $K$ to its prime field $F$ by restriction of scalars ($e:=\dim_F K$, $U_F$ the same abelian group as an $F$-vector space of dimension $e\dim_K U$), builds the generic representation $P_F(U):=(P(K\otimes_F U))_F$ over $F$ of the same degree as $P$, transports a descending chain $X_1\supseteq X_2\supseteq\ldots$ of subsets of $P$ to the chain $(X_1)_F\supseteq(X_2)_F\supseteq\ldots$ of subsets of $P_F$, applies the assumed prime-field statement, and concludes by evaluating at every $K^m$ that $X_n=X_{n_0}$ for $n\ge n_0$. That comparison of $X_n(K^m)$ with $(X_n)_F(F^m)$ through the identification $K^m=K\otimes_F F^m$, and the fact that a subset of a polynomial representation is determined by its values on the spaces $K^m$, are the substantive steps; they are short but they are not an exercise in unpacking definitions, and the proposition as stated is exactly the reduction on which a research proof of the main theorem rests. items.published_title: Robustly faithful representations of a finitely generated non-abelian free group into SL2(R) are Anosov
items.author: León Carvajales; Pablo Lessa; Rafael Potrie
items.difficulty_reason: The proof rules out a dense image by a polynomial-trace argument in which the density of finite-order traces 2cos(k pi/n) converts any dense image into an arbitrarily small unfaithful perturbation, so discreteness of the image is forced by robust faithfulness alone. It then passes to PSL2(R), uses the geometrically finite structure of the hyperbolic surface, and eliminates parabolics in two genus cases: for genus zero by perturbing a cusp generator to finite order, and for genus greater than zero by writing the cusp word as a product of commutators and simple loops and applying the retained commutator-submersion lemma to realise the perturbation while deforming only two generators. The conclusion that every element is hyperbolic then yields Anosov, equivalently quasi-isometric, in rank one. This deformation-and-surface-structure combination is research-level and clearly beyond ordinary PhD qualifying examinations in Lie theory or hyperbolic geometry.

items.difficulty_reason: The proof keeps a prescribed word omega fixed while deforming the representation: openness of the power map on loxodromic elements of SL3(R) lets the authors replace the image of one generator so that rho(a)^{-m}rho(a^m)rho(b^n) is an n-th power, which forces rho(omega) to be unchanged along the deformation. A one-parameter deformation of the unstable eigenline of rho(a) is then chosen transverse to the attracting plane, so that the coefficient functional theta_t of that plane changes sign on the two sides of t=0 while the approximating functionals of rho_t(a^p)P_0 converge to theta_t; this pins a parameter t_0 with L_0 contained in rho_{t_0}(a^p)P_0. Both rho_{t_0}(omega^q) and rho_{t_0}(a^p omega^q a^{-p}) then preserve that hyperplane and the latter acts on it as a scalar, so the commutator acts as the identity there and, having determinant one, is unipotent. This is the proposition the paper calls the main step towards its main theorem, and the simultaneous prescription-plus-transversality mechanism in a higher-rank setting is above ordinary PhD qualification problems in Lie theory or geometric group theory.

items.title: Every nonnegative discrete distribution with zero in its support is an iid-distance law on a complete separable measured metric space
items.published_title: Every nonnegative discrete distribution with zero in its support is an iid-distance law on a complete separable measured metric space
items.author: Renan Gross
items.difficulty_reason: Supplying the definition of feasibility and the elementary Bernoulli example leaves a genuinely new inverse construction: the author defines a selection space of eventually constant vectors with the index of last disagreement as distance, and must verify the triangle inequality, completeness, separability and Borel measurability under explicit subadditivity and tail-vanishing hypotheses. The proof then decomposes an arbitrary discrete law into dyadic subdistributions, telescopes the conditional probabilities beta_n so that the total mass of the non-default choices is finite, and matches both the atom at zero and every positive atom exactly. No limit of finite approximations is taken, which is precisely what keeps the space separable; this construction is above ordinary qualification probability and metric geometry.

items.title: Equiaffine immersions of closed oriented volume-preserving three-manifolds produce flat SL4/SL3 extensions and vanishing Chern–Simons invariants
items.published_title: Equiaffine immersions of closed oriented volume-preserving three-manifolds produce flat SL4/SL3 extensions and vanishing Chern–Simons invariants
items.author: Andreas Čap; Keegan J. Flood; Thomas Mettler
items.difficulty_reason: The counted proof lies above ordinary qualification differential geometry because SL(4,R)/SL(3,R) is not a symmetric space and the bracket of two transversal components has a non-zero scalar component, so the general flat-extension theorem does not apply automatically. The authors lift a volume-preserving frame to an SL(4,R) frame using the chosen transversal, recover theta=F^*(mu^top) from the volume compatibility of the immersion, and deduce flatness of the transversal connection from the volume-form lemma. They then read the transversal component of the pulled-back Maurer-Cartan equation to see that the scalar part of the bracket vanishes, which supplies the hypothesis of the counted flat-extension theorem and yields vanishing of the Chern-Simons invariant.

items.author: Matthieu Dussaule; Longmin Wang; Wenyuan Yang
items.difficulty_reason: Supplying the named Patterson--Sullivan existence, Busemann-cocycle continuity, relative Ancona and quasi-conformality prerequisites leaves a source-local partial-shadow estimate in the twisted transition-point setting: the lower bound is reduced to positive measure of a loxodromic inverse shadow combined with equivariance and the coarse Busemann cocycle, while the upper bound combines relative Ancona multiplicativity along transition points with the conical Radon--Nikodym derivative and constants uniform in r and in the group element. The mechanism is not the classical Sullivan shadow lemma: the shadows are cut out by (eta,L)-transition points, the constants must be uniform in the group element, and the authors record that the upper bound for the usual shadow remains unknown. Adapting the argument of [Yan22, Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2] to these Green-function-twisted PS measures, with Lemma 4.6 replacing Lemma 2.19 there, is above ordinary qualification hyperbolic geometry and probability.

items.published_title: Closures of higher-rank Voronoi cells for admissible discrete sets decompose into almost-orthogonal scalar Voronoi polyhedra
items.author: Omid Amini; Noema Nicolussi
items.difficulty_reason: After the elementary convexity of a higher rank Voronoi cell and the induced filtration are supplied, the authors must still recover the whole closure of the cell from the scalar Voronoi cells of the successive graded projections. The inclusion is extracted coordinate by coordinate from the lexicographic inequalities using the Lifting Lemma, and the reverse inclusion is proved through strict inequalities on products of interiors of the scalar cells, together with the translated-set reduction for a general site. The mechanism is the interaction of a lexicographic order with an almost orthogonal decomposition that need not be orthogonal, and it is precisely the structural statement explaining why higher rank Voronoi cells fail to be closed; this is research-level asymptotic convex and polyhedral geometry, not a qualification exercise.

items.difficulty_reason: Supplying the periodic-graph background still leaves a genuine source-local mechanism: the ambient space is partitioned into the facet-cone pieces attached to the faces of a triangulation of the growth polytope, and the explicit well-arranged conditions supply half-open lattice parallelepipeds on which shortest-path distances are exactly additive. The counted proof converts that additivity into the opposite-cone rational identities, and these yield both the denominator LCM description with the controlled numerator degree of the growth series and the reciprocity G_s(1/t)=(-1)^n G_s(t), with assertion (1) derived from the denominator (1-t)Q_2. This direct well-arranged-graph reciprocity argument is structurally different from the shifted-dilation Ehrhart quasipolynomial criterion and is above ordinary PhD qualifying material.

items.title: Exact minimum size of finite posets with a specified finite cyclic automorphism group
items.published_title: Exact minimum size of finite posets with a specified finite cyclic automorphism group
items.author: Barmak, Jonathan Ariel; Barreto, Agustín Nicolás
items.difficulty_reason: The counted lower bound is not a routine application of the upper-bound constructions: the proof assigns to every prime power exactly dividing n a weight on each cycle of a generator, then shows that the total weight of each prime power is at least b(p^r), by a case analysis over the exceptional orders 2,3,4,5,7 and the exception families 6, 12 and 10-14, with the correction terms 11 and 20 when 3 and 2, respectively 3 and 4, exactly divide n. Reaching that point needs the source-local structural theory of cycles of a cyclic poset automorphism, including the extension remark and the four lemmas on how many cycles of length divisible by p^r, 4 or 2p a generator must contain, each proved by constructing an extra automorphism from a symmetry or complement of the height-one posets involved. The upper bound is equally constructive, combining the b(n)n-point posets with an ordinal sum and the exceptional 20-point poset for Z_12, so the exact minus-one correction is essential; this is well above ordinary PhD qualifying material.

items.difficulty_reason: The sufficiency argument eliminates scalar intersections through a Frobenius polynomial and proves exceptionality across infinitely many field extensions. The necessity argument constructs a Kummer curve from a root, computes its genus and excludes boundary places to force a forbidden finite-field intersection by Hasse–Weil. Both directions are one restricted criterion, not separate variants.
